props.title: The Net
props.initialSlug: Nowhere to hide. Nowhere to run.

sections.content: The Net captured the mid-90s internet paranoia perfectly, arriving just as mainstream America was getting online. Sandra Bullock's isolated programmer Angela Bennett predated similar digital-identity thrillers like Enemy of the State (1998) and Hackers (1995). Its premise - that someone's entire identity could be erased and replaced digitally - seemed far-fetched to many viewers in 1995 but proved remarkably prescient about our dependence on digital systems and vulnerability to identity theft.

sections.content: Director Irwin Winkler's approach to visualizing computer use - with elaborate 3D interfaces and dramatic typing sequences - established tropes that would define how Hollywood depicted technology for years to come. While dated now, these visual flourishes in The Net influenced later films like Swordfish (2001) and Antitrust (2001), creating a specific aesthetic language for showing computer work on screen.

The film's themes of isolation and digital dependency gained new relevance during the COVID-19 pandemic, where many found themselves living Angela Bennett's work-from-home, order-everything-online lifestyle. This connection to contemporary concerns helps The Net maintain relevance despite its dated technology, similar to how WarGames (1983) still resonates through its core themes about automation and control. sections.content: The Net helped establish cyber thrillers as a viable genre, paving the way for more sophisticated explorations like Mr. Robot (2015-2019) and Searching (2018). While early entries focused on basic identity theft and system hacking, modern cyber thrillers like Unfriended (2014) and Profile (2018) reflect our more complex relationship with technology, often telling their stories entirely through computer screens.
